title: Everyday Interface as Systematic Output
original:
Related to the concept of 'system parameterisation'
Rather than directly depicting the system parameters (as data visualisation), what will be the implicit way to plot the change of data (i.e. system output parameters) subtly, poetically, metaphorically, and artistically? 

Everyday interface - not just web ui/digital interface, but literally, everyday interface that we confront - is a result of a complex system/society that we live in. No visual interface - especially if it contaminates some sort of data - can be independent from the outer world, the ever intertwined and dynamically evolving system.

Supermarket Flyer with products and pricing, for example → Pricing: Affected by economic status/policy, Product: Affected by Climate Change, Ecological System, Geopolitical status (Tariffs, etc.), Target Customers (Demographics)

Train Departure Board at Gwangmyeong Station, for example → Technology: KTX (High-speed Train), its speed, Politics: Osong station, the existence of Gwangmeong station, 지방분권/수도권 쏠림: Number of trains heading to seoul, Weather: Delay or cancellation of trains

Other gpt-generated examples (Not so impressive): 
Gas Station Price Boards
Vending Machine Inventory Displays
Digital Therometers and Air Quality Displays
Live Bus/Metro Arrival Timetables
Bank/Currency Exchange Rate Boards
Package Delivery Tracking
Restaurant Menus
"Out of Stock"
Smart Home Dashboard "Usage Graph"

What's interesting: These everyday interface represents our everyday 'normal' life, and its interface pretty much displays the same information in short-term (following 'Normal Distribution'). This is the normal 'system' we live in, where we can expect that tomorrow will be the same as today. However, in long-term and/or in Black swan, information these everyday interfaces contaminates changes vastly: Supermarket Flyer changes its products, Train Departure Board shows lots of 'cancellation', due to the act of hyperobject lying beneath the surface data/information. We prefer to call this 'abnormal', 'exception', but in reality, as the volatility/unexpectedness of the system (social, technical, ecological) that we live in becomes more complex & intertwined, these 'abnormal' situations will likely occur more often. Having everyday interface as systematic output- as the A/V output of system art -- is useful to highlight this concerning (or delighting) trend by amplifying its uncertainness/instableness. That the everyday life we know, the everyday interface we interact with, will change in a long-term consequence of our interaction.


Every visual -- every regression-to-mean visuals -- generatable and adjustable, parameterically transformed/interpretable -- representation of systematic output -- One example 태양할인마트

Data Visualisation (Dashboards, graphs) vs. Data Parameterisation → There already exists a system, operating upon parameters, and when parameters change, system functions accordingly

Simple example: 태양할인마트

Climate change —> 품목변동 —> 전단지상 물품, 농수산물 변동 
Global geopolitics —> 수출입변동 —> 품목변동 

이렇게 사소한 동네마트 전단지조차 하나의 시스템으로 Data params의 변경을 systematically plot 할수있다.

Everything can be 'everdya interface'

english:
How can a system's changing parameters appear subtly, poetically, or metaphorically, rather than as a direct data visualisation? An everyday interface offers one possibility. I mean not only a web interface, but the ordinary surfaces through which we encounter the world. These surfaces already register the complex society around them.

A supermarket flyer contains prices affected by economic conditions and policy, products shaped by climate and agriculture, and imports affected by geopolitics. Its selections also imply particular customers. A departure board at Gwangmyeong Station registers railway technology, political decisions about stations, the concentration of activity in Seoul, and weather that delays or cancels trains. What looks like a simple display is an output of many entangled systems.

In the short term, such interfaces reassure us with repetition. Tomorrow appears likely to resemble today. Over longer periods, or during a black swan event, their contents can change dramatically: familiar produce disappears from a flyer; a departure board fills with cancellations. What we call an exception makes a larger, less visible condition perceptible. An artwork could amplify this instability through the ordinary interfaces that normally make life seem predictable.

This is a distinction between visualising data and parameterising an existing visual system. In a neighbourhood supermarket flyer, interest rates could alter prices and discounts, climate could alter the available produce, and trade conditions could change the selection of imports. Even this modest printed object can become a systematic expression of changing relationships.

The vocabulary can extend to commercial interfaces, generative forms, typography, small multiples, profiles, avatars, networks, maps, and advertising. Generating these objects is increasingly easy. The more interesting problem is making them dynamic parts of a system. Both input and output could be everyday interfaces, while the system between them remains something too large to encounter directly.

Repetition offers another direction. A calendar embodies standardised social time: wages, appointments, scarcity, the feeling of being imprisoned by a schedule. What happens when calendars multiply? Could repeating this familiar system turn its authority into play, through a Warhol-like accumulation of small differences? Apartment plans and their prices suggest a related possibility for Banpo-Xism.

An interface could also detach from the product it supposedly serves: an ordinary apple presented through a luxurious commercial display. Dashboards could move between calm monitoring and breakdown. The termination of life-function displays in 2001: A Space Odyssey is an especially forceful example of a graph becoming an event.

Watching traffic from a footbridge near Hannam Bridge, I think about the flux of interface states. From above, purposeful journeys can resemble the movements of insects or particles. Every driver has somewhere to go; the distant view makes that purpose almost disappear. I am interested in holding these two perspectives together.
